To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MRI, DWI, MRS and chemical shift imaging were used to assess the outcome of 14 full-term neonates born after birth asphyxia.
the combination of DWI, localised MRS, and CSI is helpful in the evaluation of neonates with asphixia, and that the ADC values and metabolite ratios obtained with these techniques are correlated.
(1) MRI and MRS are useful for the diagnosis of brain injury in neonates with birth anoxia–ischemia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of magnetic resonance spectroscopy and chemical shift imaging to study the brain of full-term asphyxia neonates.
the study of the brain in full-term asphixiated neonates.
the use of magnetic resonance (MR) techniques to study the effects of hypoxia-ischemic brain damage in neonates and to determine their potential for the early diagnosis and prediction of outcome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MRI is a useful tool for the diagnosis of neonatal asphyxia, and that the use of DWI, MRS and especially CSI can be useful for a more precise diagnosis and prognosis.
the use of DWI, CSI and MRS is a useful and promising tool in the study of neonates with asphixia.
DWI, MRS, and CSI provide complementary data that can be useful in the assessment of brain damage and outcome prediction after neonatal hypoxic-ischaemic injury.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of DWI and MRS could improve the diagnostic accuracy for the prediction of outcome in neonates with birth anoxia.
MRS and CSI are useful in the early diagnosis of asphyxiated newborns and could provide information on the metabolic state of the brain.
DWI is a good indicator of the outcome, but the ADC value does not provide enough information to differentiate between the different types of lesions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

DWI is a useful technique in the early detection of lesions after birth anoxic-ischemia, and the combination of DWI, localised MRS (Lac/NAA and NAA/choline ratio) and CSI (Cr and NAA/chol ratio) could improve diagnostic confidence.
DWI, MRS and especially CSI are helpful in evaluating the prognosis of full-term neonates after birth asphyxia.
DWI, MRS and chemical shift imaging are complementary techniques in the diagnosis of birth asphyxia.
